Candidate-conditioned history weighting directly addresses usefulness beyond broad similarity: [DIN](https://arxiv.org/abs/1706.06978) learns a different history representation for each candidate. A lightweight adaptation is candidate-to-history cross-attention added as a residual scoring branch to SASRec, with separate query/key projections and recency features. This is an implementation hypothesis, not an established improvement on the pinned benchmark; chunk candidate scoring for full-catalog recommendations.

Relation-specific graphs offer a stronger distinction between complements and substitutes. [Transitivity-encoded graph attention networks (2024)](https://www.amazon.science/publications/transitivity-encoded-graph-attention-networks-for-complementary-item-recommendations) jointly models complementary and substitute graphs. However, the supplied histories do not identify those relations. Feasible proxies: separate directed next-item transitions from symmetric co-occurrence, retaining distinct embeddings or scoring channels. Interpret these as predictive associations, not verified complementarity; neither co-occurrence nor textual resemblance establishes functional compatibility.

Recent semantic-graph methods provide architectural ideas but often violate the pretrained-weight constraint: [SAGERec (2025)](https://www.mdpi.com/2079-9292/14/24/4844) uses pretrained LLM embeddings, while [LISRec (2026)](https://github.com/NEUIR/LISRec) filters histories through text-based item graphs and includes pretrained T5 weights. A compliant experimental alternative is locally fitted title/description TF-IDF or a jointly trained token encoder, fused through a small learned gate with ID and transition features. Preserve distinctive title tokens and model identifiers for precise entertainment/product connections. Validate each branch through macro HR@10 ablations across all four datasets; simulator feedback supplies hypotheses, not preference labels.
